section.title: The Altar of Incense and the Laver
section.sectionRationale: God adds four remaining elements to the tabernacle's furnishing and service: the golden altar of incense before the veil, the atonement money paid at every census, the bronze basin for washing before ministry, and the formulas for the sacred anointing oil and incense, both forbidden for any common use.
section.thesis: God gives instructions for the incense altar, the atonement ransom collected at every census, the basin for washing, and the exclusive formulas for the anointing oil and incense that mark everything and everyone devoted to His service as holy.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the golden altar of incense burned morning and evening; the atonement money paid so no plague comes upon the people; the bronze basin where priests wash before serving; and the sacred anointing oil and incense, reserved for the LORD alone.

media.alt: Smoke rising from a small gold altar
media.caption: Fragrant incense rises before the veil each morning and evening.

verses.text: “You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of {{incense|incense}}.
It is to be square, a cubit long, a cubit wide, and two cubits high. Its horns must be of one piece.
Overlay with pure gold the top and all the sides and horns, and make a molding of gold around it.
And make two gold rings below the molding on opposite sides to hold the poles used to carry it.
Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.
Place the altar in front of the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony, before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony, where I will meet with you.
And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps.
When Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come.
On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering; nor are you to pour a drink offering on it.

Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar. Throughout your generations he shall make atonement on it annually with the blood of the sin offering of atonement. The altar is most holy to the LORD.”

units.label: The atonement ransom
units.note: the rich shall not give more, the poor shall not give less

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a {{ransom|ransom}} for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered.
Everyone who crosses over to those counted must pay a half shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, which weighs twenty gerahs. This half shekel is an offering to the LORD.
Everyone twenty years of age or older who crosses over must give this offering to the LORD.
In making the offering to the LORD to atone for your lives, the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less.
Take the atonement money from the Israelites and use it for the service of the Tent of Meeting. It will serve as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD to make atonement for your lives.”

units.label: The bronze basin
units.note: so that they will not die

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“You are to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it,
with which Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet.
Whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister by presenting an offering made by fire to the LORD, they must wash with water so that they will not die.
Thus they are to wash their hands and feet so that they will not die; this shall be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants for the generations to come.”

units.label: The sacred anointing oil and incense
units.note: holy to the LORD, for no ordinary use

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Take the finest spices: 500 shekels of liquid myrrh, half that amount, 250 shekels, of fragrant cinnamon, 250 shekels of fragrant cane,
500 shekels of cassia, all according to the sanctuary shekel, and a hin of olive oil.
Prepare from these a sacred {{anointing|anointing oil}}, a fragrant blend, the work of a perfumer; it will be a sacred anointing oil.
Use this oil to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony,
the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense,
the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand.
You are to consecrate them so that they will be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy.
Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests.
And you are to tell the Israelites, ‘This will be My sacred anointing oil for the generations to come.
It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man, and you must not make anything like it with the same formula. It is holy, and it must be holy to you.
Anyone who mixes perfume like it or puts it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.’”
The LORD also said to Moses, “Take fragrant spices, gum resin, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, in equal measures,
and make a fragrant blend of incense, the work of a perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy.
Grind some of it into fine powder and place it in front of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you.
You are never to use this formula to make incense for yourselves; you shall regard it as holy to the LORD.
Anyone who makes something like it to enjoy its fragrance shall be cut off from his people.”

incense.gloss: Fragrant incense, burned continually on the golden altar before the veil. Its rising smoke became a common biblical picture for the prayers of God's people ascending before Him, Psalm 141:2, Revelation 8:3-4.

ransom.gloss: A ransom or price paid to cover a life, related to the word for atonement. Every Israelite counted in a census paid the same amount, rich or poor, since no one's life could be ransomed for more or less than another's before God.

anointing.gloss: The sacred anointing oil, a specific fragrant blend reserved exclusively for consecrating the tabernacle, its furnishings, and its priests. Forbidden for any ordinary use, it marked whatever it touched as set apart wholly for the LORD's service.

basic.context: God gives four remaining instructions for the tabernacle's service: a golden altar for incense burned morning and evening before the veil, a small ransom every Israelite pays at a census, a bronze basin where priests wash before ministering, and the exact, exclusive formulas for the anointing oil and incense used only for God's service.
basic.hermeneutics: These are literal, practical instructions for Israel's ongoing worship, not primarily symbols to decode. Each element serves a real function, atonement, cleansing, consecration, while also carrying meaning the rest of Scripture develops, such as incense representing prayer.
basic.originalLanguages: The qetoret, incense, rose continually before the veil, and later Scripture uses this image directly for prayer ascending to God. Every Israelite counted paid the same kopher, ransom, since atonement for a life could not be bought more cheaply or dearly depending on wealth. The shemen mishchat qodesh, sacred anointing oil, was reserved exclusively for God's service, forbidden on pain of being cut off from Israel if copied for common use.
basic.typology: The rising incense before the veil pictures the prayers of God's people ascending to Him, fulfilled as believers now pray boldly through Christ. The equal ransom paid by rich and poor alike anticipates the equal, priceless ransom Christ pays for all who trust Him, regardless of status.
basic.christ: Revelation pictures the prayers of the saints rising like incense before God's throne, Revelation 8:3-4, an image rooted directly in this altar. Paul calls Christ's death a ransom for all, 1 Timothy 2:6, echoing this chapter's ransom that could not be increased or decreased by human wealth or merit.
basic.god: God requires a ransom for every life numbered, showing that even being counted among His people carries the weight of sin needing atonement. Yet He fixes that ransom at the same small price for rich and poor alike, revealing that before Him, no one's worth or need for atonement outweighs another's.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 141:2 asks that prayer be counted as incense before God. Revelation 8:3-4 pictures the prayers of the saints rising with incense before God's throne. 1 Timothy 2:6 calls Christ's death a ransom for all people.
basic.oneStory: God ordains incense that rises continually before His presence, a ransom paid equally by every Israelite, and an anointing oil reserved exclusively for His service. Together they anticipate Christ, whose death ransoms all people equally and through whom believers' prayers now rise continually before God like fragrant incense.

context.literary:
Chapter 30 is where the long first speech of the tabernacle instructions ends and a run of shorter speeches begins. The first speech opened at Exodus 25:1, and verses 1 to 10 of this chapter are its final paragraph. Then 'the LORD said to Moses' introduces four brief speeches in quick succession, verses 11, 17, 22 and 34, before the last two in chapter 31. Four of the seven divine speeches of Exodus 25 to 31 fall in this one chapter.

The first speech has a frame. It began with the ark and the mercy seat, where God said, 'I will meet with you there,' Exodus 25:22. It closes with an altar placed 'before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony, where I will meet with you,' verse 6. The speech that designed the house begins and ends at the place of meeting. The chapter itself is framed by incense: it opens with the altar on which incense is burned, verses 1 to 10, and closes with the formula for the incense, verses 34 to 38.

Readers have long noticed that the incense altar is not described in chapters 25 and 26 with the table and lampstand, which stood beside it in the Holy Place. Its placement here ties it to the priests' daily work. Aaron has just been ordained in chapter 29, and verses 7 and 8 bind the incense to the moment 'when he tends the lamps,' morning and evening, the same rhythm as the daily lambs, Exodus 29:39.

Repetition marks the concerns of the chapter. 'Most holy' is said of the altar, verse 10, of the anointed furnishings, verse 29, and of the incense, verse 36. 'So that they will not die' is said twice of the washing, verses 20 and 21. 'Cut off from his people' closes both formulas, verses 33 and 38. The words for atonement gather in two places, the annual rite on the altar's horns, verse 10, and the census money, verses 15 and 16. Access, holiness and life are held together throughout.
context.historical:
The incense altar was small, about a foot and a half square and three feet high according to the BSB footnote to verse 2, overlaid with gold and carried on poles like the ark. Small horned altars of stone have been found at several sites in the land of Israel, and burning incense was common in the worship of the ancient world. What made Israel's altar distinct was not the practice but the place and the recipe: it stood before the veil, and only one formula could be burned on it.

The spices came from far away. Frankincense and myrrh were traded north from southern Arabia, and Jeremiah can speak of 'frankincense from Sheba or sweet cane from a distant land,' Jeremiah 6:20, naming two of the chapter's ingredients. Five hundred shekels of myrrh was roughly twelve and a half pounds. The oil and incense represented real cost and required the skill of 'a perfumer,' verses 25 and 35.

The census money was carried out almost at once. Exodus 38:25-27 records that 603,550 men 'crossed over to be numbered,' each giving 'a beka per person, that is, half a shekel,' and that the silver was cast into the hundred bases of the sanctuary and the veil. The house of God literally stood on the ransom of His people. Numbers 1:2-3 gives the census its military setting: men of twenty and over 'who can serve in Israel's army.' Later generations still knew the levy as 'the tax imposed by Moses,' 2 Chronicles 24:6. After the exile the people pledged a third of a shekel, Nehemiah 10:32, and in Jesus' day collectors asked, 'Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?' Matthew 17:24.

The bronze basin was made from 'the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,' Exodus 38:8. Polished bronze mirrors were costly personal items, and their owners gave them up to make the place where priests washed. Moses set the basin between the tent and the altar and washed there with Aaron and his sons, Exodus 40:30-32.
context.canonical:
Incense runs through the rest of Scripture as a sign both of mediation and of danger. Nadab and Abihu offered 'unauthorized fire' and died, Leviticus 10:1-2, the same word used for the 'unauthorized incense' of verse 9. On the Day of Atonement the high priest took incense inside the veil so that its cloud would cover the mercy seat 'so that he will not die,' Leviticus 16:12-13. When a plague broke out after Korah's rebellion, Aaron ran with his censer into the assembly and 'stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted,' Numbers 16:48. King Uzziah tried to burn incense on this altar and was struck with leprosy, for 'only the priests, the descendants of Aaron, are consecrated to burn incense,' 2 Chronicles 26:18-19.

Psalm 141:2 makes the link with prayer explicit, and Malachi 1:11 foresees that 'in every place, incense and pure offerings will be presented in My name' among the nations. The New Testament story opens at this altar. Zechariah was chosen 'to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense' while the people prayed outside, and an angel appeared 'at the right side of the altar of incense,' Luke 1:9-11. Revelation places the altar before God's throne, where incense rises 'together with the prayers of the saints,' Revelation 8:3-4. Hebrews 9:4 associates the golden altar with the Most Holy Place, a detail discussed below.

The census ransom is echoed in the redemption of the firstborn at five shekels each, Numbers 3:46-48, and in David's census and the plague that followed, 2 Samuel 24. Jesus speaks of giving His life 'as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and Peter reminds believers they were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The anointing oil reappears over Aaron's collar, Psalm 133:2, and its myrrh and cassia perfume the garments of the anointed king in Psalm 45:7-8, words Hebrews 1:9 applies to the Son.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses records these provisions so that Israel would understand that access to God, once opened, must be kept open every day and kept holy. The incense burns morning and evening 'for the generations to come,' verse 8; the washing is 'a permanent statute,' verse 21; the oil is God's 'for the generations to come,' verse 31. Nothing about the tabernacle was a single dedication and then silence.

He also wanted Israel to see that every counted life belonged to God. The census mustered an army, and an army is easily tempted to count its strength. By requiring a ransom for each man 'when he is counted,' verse 12, God reminded Israel that the soldiers were His, that their lives stood under judgment apart from atonement, and that a plague could come on those who forgot it. The fixed half shekel taught that rich and poor stand on the same footing before Him, verse 15.

Finally, the formulas guarded the difference between the holy and the common. Anyone who copied the oil or made the incense 'to enjoy its fragrance,' verse 38, was cut off. The first hearers were to learn that what God claims for Himself may not be turned into private pleasure, however attractive.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These are commands for Israel's sanctuary and priests. The census tax, the basin and the formulas bound Israel under the Sinai covenant, and they do not bind the church. Jesus' response to the temple tax makes this plain: 'Then the sons are exempt,' Matthew 17:26, though He paid it anyway 'so that we may not offend them.' Nor does the ban on copying the oil make perfume sinful for believers; the rule protected a sanctuary that no longer stands.

What carries forward is the shape of approach. Prayer rises before God as incense, Revelation 8:4, and should be offered as steadily as the morning and evening fire. Redemption is the same price for everyone, and in Christ 'there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free,' Galatians 3:28. Those who serve must come cleansed. And the distinction between holy and common still matters, for believers are to 'worship God acceptably with reverence and awe,' Hebrews 12:28.

debates.question: Why does God require a ransom at a census, verse 12?

views.label: Counting tempts leaders to trust in numbers
views.case: When David numbered Israel without any mention of this ransom, a plague killed seventy thousand, 2 Samuel 24:15. Many interpreters connect verse 12 with that episode: a census measures military strength, and taking it risks treating God's people as the king's resource. The ransom answers that pride with an act of atonement.

views.label: Every counted life stands under God's claim
views.case: Others see the ransom as a built-in acknowledgement rather than a response to a particular sin. To be enrolled in God's army was to be reckoned as His, and like the firstborn, Numbers 3:46-48, the numbered men had to be redeemed. The half shekel is 'a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD,' verse 16, reminding both God and people that these lives were bought.

views.label: A mystery in the account of David
views.case: 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger 'stirred up David,' while 1 Chronicles 21:1 says 'Satan rose up against Israel and incited David.' Some therefore treat David's census as a case of judgment on an already guilty nation rather than a direct commentary on Exodus 30, and caution against reading one text wholly through the other.

debates.bearing: The views are compatible. A census was a moment of danger because it drew attention to human strength and to lives God owned. The ransom kept that moment humble and safe, and the plague of 2 Samuel 24 shows what the chapter warned against.

debates.question: Did the golden altar stand in the Holy Place or belong to the Most Holy Place, given Hebrews 9:4?

views.label: Hebrews speaks of its function
views.case: Exodus 30:6 places the altar 'in front of the veil,' outside the Most Holy Place, and Exodus 40:26 confirms it. But 1 Kings 6:22 calls it 'the altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary,' and on the Day of Atonement its coals and incense went behind the veil, Leviticus 16:12-13. Hebrews says the Most Holy Place was 'containing' or 'having' the altar in the sense that the altar served that room.

views.label: Hebrews means the golden censer
views.case: The Greek word in Hebrews 9:4 can mean a censer as well as an altar of incense, and some translations render it 'golden censer.' On this view Hebrews refers to the censer the high priest carried inside the veil, not to the altar of Exodus 30.

debates.bearing: Neither view makes Hebrews contradict Exodus. The altar stood outside the veil yet belonged with the ark, facing the mercy seat 'where I will meet with you,' verse 6. That double position is exactly what makes it a fitting picture of prayer that reaches into God's presence.

debates.question: Why is the incense altar described here rather than with the other furnishings in chapters 25 and 26?

views.label: A later addition to the plan
views.case: Some critical scholars have argued that the incense altar was added to an earlier description of the tabernacle, pointing to its absence from chapters 25 and 26 where the table and lampstand appear.

views.label: A deliberate theological placement
views.case: Others note that the paragraph closes the first speech with the same phrase that opened it, 'where I will meet with you,' Exodus 25:22 and 30:6, and that it follows the ordination of chapter 29 because it describes the priest's daily service. The furniture is grouped by use, not only by room.

debates.bearing: The text as it stands gives a coherent reason for the order: the altar of incense is presented as part of the ongoing ministry of an ordained priest before the mercy seat, the point at which the plan of the house turns into the practice of worship.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'unauthorized incense' of verse 9 is qetoret zarah, and the BSB footnote gives the literal 'strange.' The adjective zar describes what is foreign or outside its proper sphere. It appears again in verse 33, where the oil must not be put 'on an outsider,' and it is the word for the 'unauthorized fire' of Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus 10:1. Numbers 18:7 warns that 'any outsider who comes near the sanctuary must be put to death.' Zar does not mean a foreigner only; it means anyone or anything not authorised for a holy place, including an Israelite who is not a priest.

The census language is military. To 'take a census' in verse 12 uses the verb paqad, to muster or number, and those counted are the pequdim. Each one 'crosses over to those counted,' verses 13 and 14, from the verb 'avar, to pass over, perhaps picturing each man stepping across to the side of the enrolled. The danger named is negeph, 'plague,' the word used at the Passover: 'No plague will fall on you to destroy you,' Exodus 12:13. The census ransom echoes the blood on the doorposts; in both, a price stands between God's people and the stroke that falls on others.

The ransom is 'for his life,' kopher nafsho, verse 12, and it atones 'for your lives,' verses 15 and 16. The same pairing of ransom and life appears when an owner may pay to 'redeem his life,' Exodus 21:30, and when the law forbids accepting 'a ransom for the life of a murderer,' Numbers 35:31. Psalm 49:7 sets the limit: 'No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God.' The Greek Old Testament renders the ransom of verse 12 with lytra, from the same family as the word Jesus uses when He gives His life 'as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45.

The priests 'wash,' rachats, their hands and feet, verses 19 to 21. The verb describes washing of the body and of sacrifices, and it gives Psalm 26:6 its image: 'I wash my hands in innocence that I may go about Your altar.' Psalm 73:13 uses the same phrase. The basin made the psalmists' language of clean hands a daily physical act.

Twice the chapter warns that an offender 'shall be cut off from his people,' verses 33 and 38, from karat, to cut. The same sanction falls on the uncircumcised, Genesis 17:14, and on the Sabbath breaker, Exodus 31:14. Interpreters differ on whether it means execution, the extinction of a family line, or a judgment God Himself carries out, but in every case the person is severed from the covenant community.

The incense is 'seasoned with salt,' memullach, verse 35. Salt was required with every grain offering as 'the salt of the covenant of your God,' Leviticus 2:13, and Numbers 18:19 calls a permanent grant 'a permanent covenant of salt.' Salt preserves and does not decay, so the incense carries the flavour of a covenant that lasts.

typology.type: The incense burning morning and evening before the veil, Exodus 30:7-8
typology.fulfillment: The smoke rose continually before the mercy seat, and on the Day of Atonement its cloud covered the mercy seat so the high priest would not die, Leviticus 16:13. Revelation shows incense rising 'together with the prayers of the saints' before God's throne, Revelation 8:4. Yet the prayers themselves rest on a greater intercession: Christ 'is at the right hand of God, and He is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34. The escalation is from a cloud that protected one man once a year to a living priest who 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25, for all who come to God through Him.

typology.type: The half shekel ransom paid by every counted man, Exodus 30:12-16
typology.fulfillment: Every man gave the same silver to ransom his life, and that silver became the bases on which the sanctuary stood, Exodus 38:27. Jesus came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, 'a ransom for all,' 1 Timothy 2:6. Peter draws the contrast: believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold' but 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type falls short because each Israelite paid for himself and paid again at the next census; in Christ the ransom is paid by another, once.

typology.type: The bronze basin for washing hands and feet, Exodus 30:18-21
typology.fulfillment: Priests already washed at their ordination, Exodus 29:4, still washed their hands and feet each time they served, 'so that they will not die.' Jesus uses the same pattern when He washes the disciples' feet: 'Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet,' John 13:10, and 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me,' John 13:8. Christ cleanses His church 'by the washing with water through the word,' Ephesians 5:26. The basin cleaned the body for a moment; Christ's washing cleanses the person and fits him for fellowship with God.

typology.type: The sacred anointing oil, forbidden on an ordinary man, Exodus 30:30-32
typology.fulfillment: The oil marked priests and furnishings as God's alone, and no ordinary man could wear it. Psalm 45:7-8 speaks of a king anointed 'with the oil of joy,' his garments 'fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia,' two of the spices of verses 23 and 24, and Hebrews 1:9 applies those words to the Son. Jesus is the Anointed One, anointed 'with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38. The escalation is that the anointing which could not be shared is now given to His people: God 'anointed us' and 'put His Spirit in our hearts,' 2 Corinthians 1:21-22.

typology.type: The yearly atonement on the horns of the altar, Exodus 30:10
typology.fulfillment: Even the altar of prayer needed blood once a year, for the sin of the people clung to the place where they approached. Hebrews notes that the high priest entered 'only once a year, and never without blood,' Hebrews 9:7. Christ 'entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12. What was annual becomes final, and prayer offered through Him no longer waits on the next Day of Atonement to be cleansed.

study.christ:
The gospel story begins at this altar. Luke opens with Zechariah chosen by lot to burn incense while 'the whole congregation was praying outside,' Luke 1:10, and the angel who announces John's birth stands 'at the right side of the altar of incense,' Luke 1:11. The prayers of generations, rising with the smoke of Exodus 30, are about to be answered in the coming of the Messiah.

Christ fulfils the altar's meaning as intercessor. Aaron once ran with his censer between the living and the dead, and the plague stopped, Numbers 16:48. Jesus stands permanently in that gap: 'He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25. The incense covered the mercy seat so the priest would not die, Leviticus 16:13. Christ's intercession covers those who come to God through Him, so that 'Who is there to condemn us?' has an answer, Romans 8:34.

He fulfils the ransom. The half shekel was the same for rich and poor because every life stood equally in need. Paul joins that equality to Christ's mediation: 'there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all,' 1 Timothy 2:5-6. There is a telling scene in Matthew 17:24-27. Asked about the temple tax, Jesus says the sons of the King are exempt, yet He provides a coin 'for My tax and yours.' The Son who owed nothing pays for Himself and for Peter together. Matthew does not call it a ransom, but it shows the Son freely standing alongside His disciple under the obligation of the sanctuary.

He fulfils the washing. At the Last Supper the Lord takes the servant's place at the basin and says, 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me,' John 13:8. The priests washed themselves; this Priest washes His people.

He fulfils the anointing. His title, Christ, means the Anointed One. The oil that could not touch an ordinary man belongs to Him, and Hebrews 1:9 hears Psalm 45's oil of joy as the Father's anointing of the Son. The spices of Exodus 30 appear around His life, frankincense and myrrh among the gifts of the Magi, Matthew 2:11, and myrrh again at His burial, John 19:39. The Gospels do not draw a symbolic line from these to Exodus, and they should not be pressed into a code. But they fit the portrait of One whose life was a 'fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2.

The chapter should not be turned into allegory at every point; the proportions of the spices and the rings of the altar have no New Testament commentary. The connections above rest on what the New Testament says about intercession, ransom, washing and anointing, the four works this chapter provides for.
study.god:
Twice in this chapter God describes the place where incense burns as the place 'where I will meet with you,' verses 6 and 36. He is not a remote deity who must be summoned. He appoints a place and a time, morning and evening, and He keeps the appointment. The whole chapter serves that meeting.

He is impartial. 'The rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less,' verse 15. Deuteronomy 10:17 calls Him the God 'showing no partiality and accepting no bribe,' and Peter learned the same truth: 'God does not show favoritism,' Acts 10:34. Before Him no one's life is worth more or less, and no one can buy a better standing.

He is the owner of every life. The census money is a 'ransom for his life,' verse 12, a reminder that the men counted as Israel's army were God's before they were Israel's. Numbering them without acknowledging that ownership invited a plague. God guards His claim on His people because it is also His protection of them.

He is holy and jealous for what is His. The oil 'is holy, and it must be holy to you,' verse 32. The incense is 'holy to the LORD,' verse 37. God does not share His signs with private use. The same holiness that makes the altar 'most holy,' verse 10, makes unauthorised incense deadly, as the deaths of Nadab and Abihu show, Leviticus 10:2.

He is also a God who delights in the senses He created. The chapter is full of fragrance: myrrh, cinnamon, cane, cassia, frankincense, galbanum, oil 'the work of a perfumer.' Worship in Israel engaged sight, smell and touch. The same God who forbade copying the fragrance for pleasure made it beautiful in the first place, and He receives what is offered to Him as a pleasing gift.

He provides the cleansing He requires. The priests must wash 'so that they will not die,' verses 20 and 21, but God supplies the basin and the water, and the women's mirrors become the means of their purity. His demands are always accompanied by His provision.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to pray steadily and without presumption, to come cleansed and not casually, to treat what God calls holy as holy, and to rest on a ransom they did not pay and could not have paid.

crossReferences.note: On the Day of Atonement the high priest takes coals and 'finely ground fragrant incense' inside the veil so that the cloud covers the mercy seat 'so that he will not die.' It shows the incense of Exodus 30:34-36 at its most solemn use, as a covering that makes approach survivable.

Nadab and Abihu offer 'unauthorized fire before the LORD' and die. The word is the one used for the 'unauthorized incense' forbidden in Exodus 30:9. The chapter's rule about what may be offered on the altar is not a technicality; it guards life.

When a plague breaks out, Aaron takes his censer with fire from the altar and incense, runs into the assembly, and 'stood between the living and the dead.' The incense that rose daily before the veil becomes the means of atonement that halts judgment.

King Uzziah enters the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense and is told 'only the priests, the descendants of Aaron, are consecrated to burn incense.' Leprosy breaks out on his forehead. The exclusivity of Exodus 30:7-9 applies even to a king.

Zechariah is chosen to burn incense while the people pray outside, and an angel appears 'at the right side of the altar of incense.' The altar of Exodus 30 is the setting for the first announcement of the gospel, as long years of prayer are answered.

An angel offers much incense 'along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne,' and the smoke rises before God. The golden altar of Exodus 30:1-6 has its heavenly counterpart, and the prayers of the church are received there.

The census silver from 603,550 men, half a shekel each, is cast into the hundred bases of the sanctuary and the veil. The ransom of Exodus 30:12-16 becomes the foundation on which the house of God literally stands.

Asked whether Jesus pays the two-drachma temple tax, the descendant of the half shekel levy, Jesus says the sons are exempt, yet provides a coin 'for My tax and yours.' The Son of the house stands with His disciple under the obligation of Exodus 30.

Believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold' but with 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.' The silver ransom of Exodus 30 is set aside in favour of a price no census could collect.

The bronze basin was made 'from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.' The detail shows the cost behind the washing of Exodus 30:18-21 and the part women played in providing for the priests' purity.

Jesus washes His disciples' feet and says, 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me,' adding that the one who has bathed needs only his feet washed. The ordination bath and the daily washing at the basin find their meaning in the washing Christ gives.

The anointed king's garments are 'fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia,' and he is anointed 'with the oil of joy.' The spices of the anointing oil in Exodus 30:23-24 perfume a royal figure whom Hebrews 1:9 identifies as the Son.

study.oneStory:
Since Eden, human beings have lived under the sentence of death and outside the presence they were made for. Exodus 30 shows the lengths to which God goes to let such people come near and live. Every piece of the chapter is about survival in His presence: incense so the priest does not die, a ransom so no plague comes, water so the priests do not die, oil and incense that must not be profaned.

The census ransom looks back to the Passover. There the blood on the doorposts meant 'no plague will fall on you to destroy you,' Exodus 12:13; here a ransom for each man means 'no plague will come upon them,' verse 12. Israel's life as a nation is held under the protection of a price paid.

The story then unfolds along the lines this chapter draws. The priests guard the incense and sometimes fail, as Nadab and Abihu do. Kings overstep, as Uzziah does. David numbers the people and a plague falls, until it is halted at the threshing floor of Araunah, 2 Samuel 24:16 and 24:25. That same threshing floor becomes the site of Solomon's temple, 2 Chronicles 3:1. The place where judgment stopped becomes the place of the altar. And the Psalms voice the problem beneath it all: 'No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God,' Psalm 49:7.

The answer comes in Christ. The Anointed One gives His life as a ransom for many, washes His people, and lives to intercede for them. The Spirit anoints the church, and prayer rises from every place, as Malachi 1:11 foresaw.

The new creation brings the chapter's provisions to their end. Revelation shows the prayers of the saints rising before the throne, Revelation 8:4, and then a city with no temple, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. There is no longer any need for a cloud of incense to shield sinners from the mercy seat, for God's servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. What the high priest could approach only under a covering, the whole people of God will look upon openly.

quiz.q: When was Aaron to burn the fragrant incense on the golden altar?

options.text: Every morning and at twilight, perpetually before the LORD.
options.note: Verses 7 to 8 specify this continual, twice daily pattern.

options.text: Only once a year, on the Day of Atonement.
options.note: The annual atonement on the altar's horns, verse 10, was separate from the regular morning and evening incense burning.

options.text: Whenever an individual worshiper requested it.
options.note: The incense schedule was fixed by God, tied to the tending of the lamps, not left to individual request.

options.text: No regular schedule is given.
options.note: Verses 7 to 8 explicitly establish a morning and evening pattern.

quiz.q: How much was each Israelite required to pay as atonement money at a census, according to verse 15?

options.text: A half shekel, the same amount for rich and poor alike.
options.note: Verse 15 states explicitly that the rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less.

options.text: An amount proportional to each person's wealth.
options.note: The text explicitly rejects a wealth-based sliding scale; the amount was fixed and equal.

options.text: A full shekel from every household.
options.note: The specified amount was a half shekel per individual, not a full shekel per household.

options.text: No payment was required.
options.note: Verses 12 through 15 explicitly require this atonement payment.

quiz.q: Why did Aaron and his sons need to wash their hands and feet at the bronze basin?

options.text: So that they would not die when entering the Tent of Meeting or approaching the altar.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21 give this exact, sober reason twice.

options.text: Simply as a matter of personal hygiene.
options.note: While washing has hygienic benefit, the text specifically frames this as a matter of life and death before God, not mere hygiene.

options.text: To prepare their appearance before the people.
options.note: The stated purpose concerns approaching God at the altar and tent, not their appearance before the congregation.

options.text: No reason is given for the washing.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21 explicitly state the reason: so that they will not die.

quiz.q: What was forbidden regarding the sacred anointing oil, according to verses 32 to 33?

options.text: It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man, nor could anyone make anything like it with the same formula.
options.note: Verses 32 to 33 explicitly state this prohibition, with a penalty of being cut off from the people.

options.text: It could be freely sold to any Israelite family.
options.note: The text explicitly prohibits common use or replication of the oil, not permits its sale.

options.text: It could be used, but only by the wealthy.
options.note: The prohibition applies to any ordinary use regardless of wealth, not merely a restriction based on economic status.

options.text: No restrictions were placed on the oil's use.
options.note: Verses 32 to 33 explicitly restrict the oil's use to sacred purposes alone.

quiz.q: What penalty is given for making incense like the sacred formula simply to enjoy its fragrance?

options.text: Being cut off from his people.
options.note: Verse 38 states this exact penalty.

options.text: A fine paid in silver.
options.note: The stated penalty is being cut off from the community, not a monetary fine.

options.text: Temporary exclusion from the camp for seven days.
options.note: The text specifies being cut off from the people, a far more severe and permanent consequence than a temporary exclusion.

options.text: No penalty is mentioned.
options.note: Verse 38 explicitly states the penalty of being cut off from the people.

questions: Incense rose before God morning and evening without fail, later pictured as the prayers of His people. How consistent is your own pattern of prayer, morning and evening, compared to this continual rhythm?

The atonement ransom was the same for the richest and poorest Israelite alike. Where might you be tempted to think your standing before God depends on what you have achieved or accumulated, rather than on Christ's equal ransom for all?
Aaron and his sons had to wash before every act of service, not just once at ordination. What ongoing, regular practices of confession and cleansing do you build into your own walk with God?
The anointing oil and incense were reserved exclusively for God, never to be copied for ordinary enjoyment. Where do you see the sacred and the ordinary blurred together in your own life or worship?

God required atonement simply for the Israelites being counted among His people. How does remembering that even being numbered among God's people required atonement shape your sense of what it cost for you to belong to Him?

translationNotes.note: Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar refers to the Day of Atonement ritual detailed later in Leviticus 16:18-19, distinct from the daily incense offering described in the earlier verses of this chapter.
The census ransom described here is later carried out in Numbers 1:1-3, 46, where the total silver collected corresponds to the exact half shekel per counted man commanded in this passage.

Onycha and galbanum are aromatic substances whose precise ancient identity is debated among scholars, though their general character as fragrant resins used in perfumery is well attested in the ancient Near East.
